items.claim: Blues grew among African Americans in the Deep South after the end of slavery
items.note: Hedge dropped: intro says its first appearance 'is often dated to after the ending of slavery'; Origin says dating is 'usually' after 1863 and the causes 'are not fully known'.

fix.text: Blues grew among African Americans in the Deep South, usually dated to the decades after slavery ended, out of work songs, field hollers, spirituals and ballads. Its call-and-response phrasing, blue notes and twelve-bar form run all through jazz, rhythm and blues and rock and roll.

items.claim: women singers from vaudeville were the first blues stars on record ... led a wave that sold to Black and white buyers alike
items.note: Two stretches. The section says classic female and vaudeville blues singers 'were popular in the 1920s' and Mamie Smith was the first African American to record a blues song; it does not call the women the first blues stars on record. It says 'some' of their records 'were purchased by white buyers as well', not 'Black and white buyers alike'.

fix.text: In the 1920s women singers, many from vaudeville, were the blues' big stars on record. Ma Rainey, the 'Mother of the Blues', and Bessie Smith were two of 'the big three', and some of their records sold to white buyers too.

items.claim: Muddy Waters made Chicago a centre for this louder sound
items.note: Causation added: the section says 'Chicago became a center for electric blues from 1948 on, when Muddy Waters recorded his first success'. A timing link, not that he made it so.

fix.text: After the war, migrants from Mississippi plugged in: electric guitar, harmonica through a microphone, bass and drums. Chicago became a centre for this louder sound from 1948, when Muddy Waters had his first hit there, and it later fired up British bands such as the Rolling Stones. B. B. King's string-bending solos went on to shape electric blues guitar.

items.note: Jazz intro says this of 'New Orleans jazz' and adds in the next sentence that 'jazz did not begin as a single musical tradition in New Orleans or elsewhere'. Stating it of jazz as a whole drops that hedge.

fix.text: New Orleans jazz mixed brass-band marches, ragtime and blues with group improvisation, and blues forms and blue notes stayed at its heart.

items.claim: Duke Ellington preferred to call his work American music, 'beyond category'
items.cited: genre sources: Jazz Infobox, intro, Improvisation
items.note: Not in any cited section. The corpus has it elsewhere and it says something different: Ellington 'called his music American Music, rather than jazz, and liked to describe those who impressed him as "beyond category"' (The influence of Duke Ellington). fix.text: Jazz is famously hard to define: one writer calls it 'a construct' for many related musics, and Duke Ellington called his own work American Music rather than jazz.

items.claim: Swing: a rhythmic lilt that makes even, steady notes feel bouncy and alive.
items.cited: Jazz intro; Swing in the early 20th century
items.note: The section describes swing as triple subdivisions of the beat laid over a duple (even) pulse. Saying swing makes 'even' notes feel bouncy can mislead a newcomer into thinking the notes stay even; the point is that they don't.

fix.text: Swing: instead of splitting each beat evenly, players split it unevenly, in threes over a steady pulse, so the music rolls and bounces.

fix.text: Instruments talking to each other, from New Orleans players weaving countermelodies around the tune to call and response in the vocals.

items.claim: Swing fans were often hostile at first.
items.note: Section: 'a divided, sometimes hostile response among fans and musicians, especially swing players'. 'Often' strengthens 'sometimes', and the hostility it singles out is from swing players, not swing fans.

fix.text: In the 1940s bebop players such as Charlie Parker made jazz music for listening, not dancing: faster tempos, trickier chords and racing lines. The response was divided and sometimes hostile, especially from swing players, but by the 1950s bebop was part of the jazz vocabulary.

items.claim: his In a Silent Way went electric and opened the door to fusion
items.cited: Jazz Modal jazz; Miles Davis's new directions
items.note: Section says In a Silent Way 'can be considered his first fusion album' (hedged, about his own work). 'Opened the door to fusion' implies it started the genre; the intro dates fusion's appearance to the late 1960s generally, and the same section names Tony Williams Lifetime's Emergency! (1969) as another early fusion album.

fix.text: Miles Davis's Kind of Blue (1959) built solos on scales rather than fast-changing chords, and became the best-selling jazz album. A decade later he went fully electric with In a Silent Way (1969), which can be considered his first fusion album.
